name: Iron smelting
what: Smelting iron ore into bloomery iron, later steel and (in China) cast iron.
why: Iron ore is common where copper and tin are rare, so iron tools and weapons were cheap enough for farmers and ordinary soldiers, not just palaces.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Iron Age
Wikipedia: Ferrous metallurgy
Wagner, D. B. (1993). Iron and Steel in Ancient China. Brill.
Alpern, S. B. (2005). Did they or didn't they invent it? Iron in sub-Saharan Africa. History in Africa 32, 41-94.

name: War chariot
what: A light two-wheeled cart with spoked wheels, pulled by horses, used as a fighting platform.
why: For about 500 years whoever had chariots and trained horses dominated open battlefields from Egypt to China.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Chariot
Anthony, D. W. (2007). The Horse, the Wheel, and Language. Princeton University Press.

name: Domestic horse (DOM2)
what: The horse lineage that all modern domestic horses descend from, bred on the lower Volga-Don steppe.
why: Horses multiplied the speed of armies, messengers and migrants; they also rebuilt the Great Plains when they returned to the Americas.

sources.cite: Librado, P. et al. (2021). The origins and spread of domestic horses from the Western Eurasian steppes. Nature 598, 634-640.
Wikipedia: Domestication of the horse

name: Stirrup
what: A loop hung from the saddle to hold the rider's foot; the paired metal stirrup is a Chinese invention.
why: It made mounted shock combat and heavy cavalry easier; Lynn White's claim that it created feudalism is now widely rejected.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Stirrup
Dien, A. E. (1986). The stirrup and its effect on Chinese military history. Ars Orientalis 16, 33-56.
White, L. (1962). Medieval Technology and Social Change. Oxford.

name: Papermaking
what: Making sheets from macerated plant fibre (hemp, rags, bark) on a screen.
why: Paper was cheaper than silk, parchment or bamboo, and it carried bureaucracies, scholarship and later the printing press.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: History of paper
Bloom, J. (2001). Paper Before Print: The History and Impact of Paper in the Islamic World. Yale.
Tsien Tsuen-hsuin (1985). Paper and Printing. Science and Civilisation in China 5.1. Cambridge.

name: Printing press
what: Woodblock printing in China, movable type in China and Korea, and Gutenberg's press with metal type in Mainz.
why: By 1500 European presses had produced millions of books; printing spread the Reformation and the scientific revolution faster than censors could follow.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Global spread of the printing press
Eisenstein, E. L. (1979). The Printing Press as an Agent of Change. Cambridge.
Febvre, L. & Martin, H.-J. (1958). L'Apparition du livre. Albin Michel.

name: Gunpowder & guns
what: A mix of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal, first a Chinese alchemists' discovery, then fire lances, bombs and metal-barrelled guns.
why: Guns and cannon remade war and states: walls that stood for centuries fell, and empires that could pay for artillery grew.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: History of gunpowder
Andrade, T. (2016). The Gunpowder Age: China, Military Innovation, and the Rise of the West. Princeton.
Needham, J. (1986). Science and Civilisation in China 5.7: The Gunpowder Epic. Cambridge.

name: Magnetic compass
what: A magnetised needle that points north, first described in Song China.
why: Pilots could hold a course under cloud and out of sight of land, which opened the open-ocean routes of the 15th and 16th centuries.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Compass
Needham, J. (1962). Science and Civilisation in China 4.1: Physics. Cambridge.

name: Watermill
what: A wheel turned by flowing water to grind grain, full cloth, saw wood or work bellows.
why: The first big source of non-muscle power; by 1086 England had over 5,600 mills.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Watermill
Lucas, A. (2006). Wind, Water, Work: Ancient and Medieval Milling Technology. Brill.

name: Windmill
what: Sails that turn a shaft with the wind: vertical-axis panemone mills in Persia, horizontal-axis post mills in Europe.
why: Wind power drained the Low Countries and ground grain where rivers were weak or froze.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Windmill
Lucas, A. (2006). Wind, Water, Work. Brill.

name: Steam engine
what: An engine that turns the heat of burning coal into work: Newcomen's atmospheric engine, then Watt's separate condenser.
why: It unlocked fossil energy for pumping, factories, ships and railways, the core of the Industrial Revolution.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Newcomen atmospheric engine
Wikipedia: Watt steam engine
Allen, R. C. (2009). The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective. Cambridge.

name: Semaphore telegraph
what: Chains of towers passing coded signals by moving arms, read by telescope.
why: The first state network that moved messages faster than a horse, from the French Revolution to the 1840s.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Semaphore line

name: Steamship
what: Ships driven by steam engines, first on rivers, then across oceans.
why: Steam made sailing times regular and independent of the wind; with the Suez Canal it cut Europe-Asia voyages from months to weeks.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Steamship
Wikipedia: Suez Canal

name: Railway
what: Steam locomotives on iron rails; country steps after the curated ones come from the first year with track open in Comin and Hobijn's HCCTA dataset.
why: Railways cut land freight costs several-fold, tied markets together and made famine relief and mass armies possible.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: History of rail transport

Comin, D. & Hobijn, B. (2004). Cross-country technology adoption: making the theories face the facts. Journal of Monetary Economics 51, 39-83 (HCCTA dataset, from Mitchell, International Historical Statistics).

name: Electric telegraph
what: Messages sent as electric pulses over wire, then undersea cable.
why: For the first time news moved faster than people: London-Bombay went from weeks to the same day in 1870.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Electrical telegraph
Wikipedia: Transatlantic telegraph cable
Kaukiainen, Y. (2001). Shrinking the world: improvements in the speed of information transmission, c. 1820-1870. European Review of Economic History 5, 1-28.

name: Electric power station
what: Central stations that generate electricity and sell it over wires.
why: Electricity moved energy as easily as the telegraph moved news, and let factories put a motor on every machine.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Pearl Street Station
Wikipedia: Holborn Viaduct power station

name: Motor car
what: Road vehicles with internal-combustion engines; country counts come from HCCTA (private cars, thousands).
why: Cars and trucks made oil the leading energy source and rebuilt cities around roads.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Benz Patent-Motorwagen
Wikipedia: Ford Model T

name: Haber-Bosch fertiliser
what: Making ammonia from air and natural gas at high pressure, the source of synthetic nitrogen fertiliser.
why: Synthetic nitrogen feeds roughly half of humanity; without it the 20th-century population boom could not have been fed.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Haber process
Smil, V. (2001). Enriching the Earth. MIT Press.
Erisman, J. W. et al. (2008). How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world. Nature Geoscience 1, 636-639.

name: Green Revolution seeds
what: Semi-dwarf, fertiliser-responsive wheat and rice varieties, with irrigation and synthetic nitrogen.
why: Cereal yields in much of Asia and Latin America doubled or tripled after 1960, against forecasts of mass famine.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Green Revolution
Evenson, R. E. & Gollin, D. (2003). Assessing the impact of the Green Revolution, 1960 to 2000. Science 300, 758-762.

name: Wheat
what: Einkorn and emmer wheat, domesticated in the northern Fertile Crescent; bread wheat followed.
why: The staple of West Asian, European and North Indian civilisations; where wheat went, cities and taxes followed.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Wheat
Zohary, D., Hopf, M. & Weiss, E. (2012). Domestication of Plants in the Old World, 4th ed. Oxford.

name: Rice
what: Asian rice (Oryza sativa) from the Yangtze, and a separate African rice (O. glaberrima) from the inner Niger delta.
why: Wet rice feeds more people per hectare than any other grain, which made South China, Java and Bengal the most densely settled lands on earth.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Rice
Fuller, D. Q. et al. (2009). The domestication process and domestication rate in rice. Science 323, 1607-1610.

name: Maize
what: Corn, bred from teosinte grass in the Balsas valley of Mexico.
why: The base of Mesoamerican and Andean civilisation; after 1492 it spread across Africa, southern Europe and China.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Maize
Matsuoka, Y. et al. (2002). A single domestication for maize shown by multilocus microsatellite genotyping. PNAS 99, 6080-6084.

name: Potato
what: Tubers domesticated in the Andes near Lake Titicaca.
why: Calorie-rich and easy to grow on poor soil; Nunn and Qian estimate it explains about a quarter of Old World population growth 1700-1900.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: History of the potato
Nunn, N. & Qian, N. (2011). The potato's contribution to population and urbanization. QJE 126, 593-650.

name: Cassava
what: Manioc, a starchy root domesticated in the southwestern Amazon.
why: Grows in poor soil and survives drought; it became Africa's most important food crop.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Cassava
Olsen, K. M. & Schaal, B. A. (1999). Evidence on the origin of cassava. PNAS 96, 5586-5591.
Jones, W. O. (1959). Manioc in Africa. Stanford.

name: Sugarcane
what: A giant grass domesticated in New Guinea; Indians learned to crystallise its juice into sugar.
why: Sugar plantations drove the Atlantic slave trade: most of the 12.5 million Africans shipped across the Atlantic went to sugar colonies.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: History of sugar
Mintz, S. (1985). Sweetness and Power. Viking.
Eltis, D. & Richardson, D. (2010). Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade. Yale.

name: Coffee
what: Arabica coffee from the Ethiopian highlands, first brewed by Sufis in Yemen.
why: Coffeehouses became places of news, trade and politics from Istanbul to London; plantations remade Java and Brazil.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: History of coffee
Hattox, R. S. (1985). Coffee and Coffeehouses. University of Washington Press.

name: Tea
what: Leaves of Camellia sinensis, native to the hills of Yunnan and its neighbours.
why: Tea paid for Britain's trade with China, helped cause the Opium War, and turned Assam and Ceylon into plantation economies.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: History of tea
Mair, V. & Hoh, E. (2009). The True History of Tea. Thames & Hudson.

name: Columbian Exchange
what: The transfer of crops, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492.
why: Maize, potatoes and cassava fed Old World population growth; wheat, sugar, horses and cattle remade the Americas; Old World diseases killed most Native Americans.

sources.cite: Crosby, A. W. (1972). The Columbian Exchange. Greenwood.
Nunn, N. & Qian, N. (2010). The Columbian Exchange: a history of disease, food, and ideas. Journal of Economic Perspectives 24, 163-188.
